newsitem.title: MEXICO: Witness says Mexican planes carried bribes.
newsitem.headline: Witness says Mexican planes carried bribes.

text.p: A former Mexican federal police officer on Tuesday said government airplanes were routinely used to ferry millions of dollars in bribes to high-level officials in Mexico City.

Caesar Dominguez Becerra, a former member of the Mexican federal police who also was a paid informant for U.S. agents, said he collected boxes and bags filled with cash from traffickers operating along the U.S.-Mexico border and loaded the money onto planes bound for the headquarters of the Federal Attorney General's Office, or PGR.
"On some occasions it was to pick up money, on some occasions it was to pick up drugs," Dominguez said of his duties as a police officer.

In separate testimony, convicted trafficker Juan Antonio Ortiz, once a top lieutenant in the Gulf drug cartel based in northern Mexico said bribes were paid "all the way to the top in Mexico City" for protection.

The testimony came in the second day of a civil case in which prosecutors are trying to confiscate $9 million from a Texas bank account controlled by Mario Ruiz Massieu, a former deputy attorney general who fled Mexico in 1995.

Dominguez testified he was personally involved in collecting boxes filled with cash from major drug traffickers operating out of Juarez, including Amado Carrillo Fuentes, the so-called "Lord of the Skies," and his cousin Miguel Zaragosa Fuentes.
Dominguez also said he participated in torturing traffickers who refused to pay bribes to police.
"If someone did not pay their quota, then we had to pressure them," he said. "Sometimes I used the buzzer," he said, referring to an electrical prod attached to the victim's testicles.

Ortiz, now locked away in a U.S. prison, said the Gulf cartel headed by convicted drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego also spent vast sums of money on bribes to buy law enforcement complicity in shipping Colombian cocaine to the United States.
He said he believed every law enforcement official in Mexico was corrupt.

"Luis Medrano (another cartel insider) told me, 'don't worry as far as law enforcement, we've got it all under control, all the way to the top,'" he said. "Medrano gave me assurances that money was being paid all the way to the top in Mexico City...it was being paid all the way to the Attorney General's office."
Ortiz admitted he had no direct knowledge of payments the Gulf cartel made to Ruiz Massieu, but had been told "everybody was being paid."
"Even the President of Mexico?" asked Kathy Fleming, a Ruiz Massieu attorney.
"I said everybody," Ortiz responded before quickly backpedaling to say that he knew only about the cartel's links to law enforcement, not politicians.

Garcia Abrego, who was on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list before his capture in January 1996, was convicted on drug charges here last October and is serving a life sentence without parole in a U.S. prison.

Ruiz Massieu attorney Tony Canales in opening arguments on Monday said his client's account in Texas Commerce Bank was not drug money, but a family fortune placed in the United States for safekeeping.

But in court documents obtained on Tuesday, prosecutors said they plan to call witnesses who will testify that Ruiz Massieu personally received proceeds from a nearly 10-ton shipment of cocaine seized and then sold by police in 1994 in the northern state of Zacatecas.
Another witness will say that a police commandere arrested in June 1994 said he was carrying $300,000 "intended for Massieu," the documents said.
